title: Health Systems
subtitle: Navigate French healthcare, weigh bioethical arguments and talk about mental health with care

lessons.title: La Sécurité sociale
lessons.description: How French healthcare actually works day to day: the carte Vitale, your médecin traitant, what gets reimbursed and what your mutuelle picks up.

blocks.heading: "La Sécu" — one system, two layers
blocks.body: French healthcare runs on two layers stacked on top of each other. The first is l'Assurance maladie, the public branch of la Sécurité sociale, funded by cotisations taken from salaries and by tax. It reimburses a fixed share of each consultation or medicine — typically 70 % of the official tariff for a GP visit. The remainder, called le ticket modérateur, is what your private top-up insurance, la mutuelle, is there to cover. Almost everyone talks about "la Sécu" in conversation; "la Sécurité sociale" is the written, administrative form.

examples.english: The state health insurance reimburses seventy percent of the agreed tariff.

blocks.tip: "Le reste à charge" — literally "the remainder to be borne" — is the single most useful phrase in any French discussion about health costs.

blocks.heading: La carte Vitale and le tiers payant
blocks.body: The carte Vitale is a green chip card holding your insurance rights. You hand it over at the pharmacy or the surgery, it is read by a small terminal, and the reimbursement is triggered automatically — no paperwork, money back in your account within days. Where le tiers payant applies, you do not even advance the money: the pharmacist or doctor bills l'Assurance maladie directly. When the card cannot be read, the practitioner gives you une feuille de soins on paper, which you post to your caisse yourself.

examples.french: Le remboursement arrive généralement sous cinq jours.
examples.english: The reimbursement usually arrives within five days.

blocks.tip: Update the card free of charge at the small green terminal in most pharmacies — after a move, a birth or a change of job.

blocks.heading: Le médecin traitant and le parcours de soins
blocks.body: Every adult is expected to declare a médecin traitant, a named GP who coordinates their care. Going through this declared doctor is called respecting le parcours de soins coordonné. Consult a specialist directly, without a referral, and you are still seen — but reimbursed at a much lower rate. A handful of specialities are hors parcours by law and can be consulted freely, among them gynaecology, ophthalmology and psychiatry for younger patients.

blocks.heading: The administrative passive — and how to dodge it
blocks.body: French officialese loves the passive: "vous serez remboursé", "les frais sont pris en charge", "votre demande a été enregistrée". Learn to read it fluently, because every letter from your caisse is written that way. In speech, though, French prefers two lighter constructions: "on" plus an active verb, and se faire / se voir plus an infinitive. "Je me suis fait rembourser" and "il s'est vu refuser la prise en charge" both keep the subject in place while the action is done to them.

examples.french: Votre dossier a été transmis au service médical.
examples.english: Your file has been forwarded to the medical department.
examples.note: written register — typical of an official letter

examples.french: On vous remboursera sous cinq jours.
examples.english: You'll be reimbursed within five days.

examples.french: Je me suis fait rembourser sans problème.
examples.english: I got reimbursed without any trouble.
examples.note: se faire + infinitive — the speaker triggered the action

examples.french: Elle s'est vu refuser le tiers payant.
examples.english: She was refused direct billing.
examples.note: se voir + infinitive — the past participle "vu" stays invariable here

examples.french: Les remboursements sont effectués par virement.
examples.english: Reimbursements are made by bank transfer.

examples.french: Le patient s'est fait adresser à un cardiologue.
examples.english: The patient was referred to a cardiologist.

blocks.tip: Rule of thumb: read the passive, speak with "on" or "se faire". Using officialese out loud sounds like you are quoting a form.

blocks.heading: Conditions: sous réserve de, à condition que, en cas de
blocks.body: Entitlements always come with conditions attached, and French has a precise toolkit for them. Before a noun, use en cas de and sous réserve de — no verb needed. Before a clause, à condition que and pourvu que take the subjunctive, while si takes the indicative. If both clauses share a subject, prefer the lighter à condition de plus an infinitive.

examples.english: In the event of hospitalisation, notify your top-up insurer.

examples.english: As long as the deadline is respected, the request will be processed.

blocks.tip: "Sous réserve de" is the polite administrative hedge par excellence — it lets an official promise nothing while sounding helpful.

passages.title: Première visite chez le médecin
passages.french:
Installée en France depuis six semaines, Rana s'assoit dans la salle d'attente d'un cabinet médical de quartier.
La secrétaire lui demande sa carte Vitale ; Rana n'en a pas encore, seulement une attestation provisoire de droits.
« Ce n'est pas grave, la rassure-t-elle. Vous réglez la consultation aujourd'hui et le docteur vous remettra une feuille de soins. »
Le généraliste la reçoit vingt minutes plus tard. Il l'écoute, l'examine, puis lui explique le système en deux phrases.
« Ici, tout passe par le médecin traitant. Si vous me déclarez comme tel, vous serez remboursée à soixante-dix pour cent. »
Rana hésite : elle a entendu dire qu'il fallait attendre des mois pour voir un spécialiste.
« C'est vrai dans certaines spécialités, reconnaît-il, mais je peux vous adresser directement à un confrère si nécessaire. »
Il remplit le formulaire de déclaration, qu'elle signe, et lui tend une ordonnance ainsi que la feuille de soins.
« Envoyez-la à votre caisse d'assurance maladie. Sous réserve que le dossier soit complet, le remboursement arrivera vite. »
À la pharmacie, on lui demande de nouveau sa carte. Elle explique, on lui sourit : la situation est banale.
Une franchise d'un euro par boîte est retenue, précise le pharmacien, et le reste sera couvert dès qu'elle aura une mutuelle.
Trois semaines plus tard, Rana reçoit sa carte Vitale par courrier, avec une lettre entièrement rédigée au passif.
Elle n'en comprend pas chaque mot, mais elle reconnaît l'essentiel : « vos droits ont été ouverts ».
Et, pour la première fois depuis son arrivée, l'administration française lui paraît presque accueillante.
passages.english:
Living in France for six weeks, Rana sits down in the waiting room of a neighbourhood surgery.
The receptionist asks for her carte Vitale; Rana doesn't have one yet, only a temporary statement of entitlements.
"That's not a problem," she reassures her. "You pay for the consultation today and the doctor will give you a paper claim form."
The GP sees her twenty minutes later. He listens to her, examines her, then explains the system in two sentences.
"Here, everything goes through the family doctor. If you declare me as yours, you'll be reimbursed at seventy percent."
Rana hesitates: she has heard that you have to wait months to see a specialist.
"That's true in certain specialities," he admits, "but I can refer you directly to a colleague if necessary."
He fills in the declaration form, which she signs, and hands her a prescription along with the claim form.
"Send it to your health insurance fund. Provided the file is complete, the reimbursement will arrive quickly."
At the pharmacy, she is asked for her card again. She explains, they smile at her: the situation is entirely ordinary.
A one-euro deductible per box is withheld, the pharmacist points out, and the rest will be covered once she has top-up insurance.
Three weeks later, Rana receives her carte Vitale in the post, with a letter written entirely in the passive.
She doesn't understand every word, but she recognises the essential part: "your entitlements have been opened".
And, for the first time since she arrived, French administration strikes her as almost welcoming.

lessons.title: Éthique médicale
lessons.description: The vocabulary and argumentative moves of French bioethics debates: consent, end of life and organ donation — presented from several sides.

blocks.heading: Le consentement éclairé
blocks.body: The cornerstone of French medical law is consent: no procedure without the patient's informed agreement. "Éclairé" means the patient has been given the information needed to decide — risks, alternatives, likely outcomes. The same law lets a patient refuse treatment, and lets them appoint une personne de confiance to speak for them if they can no longer speak for themselves. In debate, the recurring tension is between autonomie (the patient decides) and the doctor's duty of care.

examples.french: Aucun acte médical ne peut être pratiqué sans consentement.
examples.english: No medical procedure may be carried out without consent.

examples.french: Le consentement doit être libre et éclairé.
examples.english: Consent must be free and informed.

examples.french: L'autonomie du patient prime sur l'avis du médecin.

blocks.tip: "Éclairé" is worth its own note: it describes the decision, not the person. Never translate it as "clever".

blocks.heading: La fin de vie — a debate, not a verdict
blocks.body: France distinguishes carefully between several notions, and the vocabulary matters more than the opinions. Soins palliatifs relieve suffering without hastening death. Directives anticipées record in advance what treatment you would accept. Acharnement thérapeutique — now called obstination déraisonnable in law — means continuing treatment beyond any benefit. Euthanasie and suicide assisté designate acts that remain prohibited in France, and are precisely what successive parliamentary debates are about. Positions differ sharply and reasonable people land in different places.

examples.french: Ses directives anticipées étaient très claires.

blocks.tip: In an exam or a discussion, attribute positions rather than asserting them: "selon ses partisans", "pour ses détracteurs".

blocks.heading: Le don d'organes and le consentement présumé
blocks.body: French law works on présomption de consentement: everyone is deemed a donor unless they registered a refusal on the registre national des refus. The principles taught alongside it are gratuité (no payment for organs) and anonymat (donor and recipient are not told each other's identity). Even so, families are consulted, and the gap between the legal rule and daily practice is itself a classic debate topic.

blocks.heading: Conceding a point: bien que, quoique, même si
blocks.body: A balanced argument concedes before it objects, and French marks the concession explicitly. Bien que and quoique take the subjunctive; même si and alors que take the indicative — a distinction that trips up almost every learner. When the two clauses share a subject, bien que plus a bare adjective or participle is idiomatic and elegant: "bien que favorable au texte, il reste prudent". Sans que also takes the subjunctive and often replaces an English "without".

blocks.heading: Attributing an opinion instead of asserting it
blocks.body: In a bioethics discussion you constantly report positions you do not necessarily hold. French gives you three tools. Selon plus a noun attributes cleanly. The conditional — often called the conditionnel journalistique — signals that a claim is not verified. And a set of verbs of opinion put the subjunctive under negation or interrogation: "je ne pense pas que ce soit", but "je pense que c'est".

passages.title: Une séance du comité d'éthique
passages.french:
La salle est petite, la table ovale, et personne ne hausse la voix : un comité d'éthique ne ressemble pas à un plateau de télévision.
À l'ordre du jour, une question que le comité examine pour la quatrième fois en dix ans : faut-il modifier la loi sur la fin de vie ?
Une juriste ouvre la séance en rappelant l'état du droit, sans donner son avis personnel.
« La loi actuelle interdit l'obstination déraisonnable et autorise une sédation profonde dans des cas strictement définis. »
Un médecin de soins palliatifs prend la parole. Selon lui, l'urgence serait ailleurs : dans l'inégalité d'accès aux services existants.
« Vingt-six départements n'ont pas d'unité dédiée. Bien que le débat porte sur la loi, la réalité se joue dans les moyens. »
Une philosophe lui répond que l'argument des moyens ne clôt pas la discussion de principe.
« On peut améliorer l'accompagnement et continuer de s'interroger sur l'autonomie de la personne. Les deux ne s'excluent pas. »
Un infirmier rappelle que les équipes vivent ces dilemmes chaque semaine, et qu'aucun texte ne les supprimera.
Une représentante d'association insiste, elle, sur les directives anticipées, encore rédigées par une minorité de patients.
« Tant que les gens n'écrivent pas leurs volontés, ce sont les familles qui portent le poids de la décision. »
Personne ne conclut. Le comité rendra un avis, prudent, assorti d'opinions divergentes annexées au texte.
C'est peut-être la seule chose sur laquelle tout le monde s'accorde ce matin-là : la nuance n'est pas une faiblesse.
Et le désaccord, correctement formulé, reste la manière la plus honnête d'avancer.
passages.english:
The room is small, the table oval, and nobody raises their voice: an ethics committee looks nothing like a television panel.
On the agenda, a question the committee is examining for the fourth time in ten years: should the end-of-life law be changed?
A lawyer opens the session by setting out the state of the law, without giving her personal opinion.
"The current law prohibits unreasonable persistence in treatment and permits deep sedation in strictly defined cases."
A palliative care doctor speaks. In his view, the urgency lies elsewhere: in unequal access to the services that already exist.
"Twenty-six départements have no dedicated unit. Although the debate is about the law, reality is decided by resources."
A philosopher replies that the resources argument does not close the discussion of principle.
"We can improve support and go on questioning the person's autonomy. The two are not mutually exclusive."
A nurse points out that teams live these dilemmas every week, and that no legal text will abolish them.
A representative of a patients' association stresses advance directives, still written by only a minority of patients.
"As long as people don't write down their wishes, it is families who carry the weight of the decision."
Nobody concludes. The committee will issue an opinion, a cautious one, with dissenting views appended to the text.
That is perhaps the only thing everyone agrees on that morning: nuance is not a weakness.
And disagreement, properly expressed, remains the most honest way of moving forward.

lessons.title: Santé mentale
lessons.description: How to talk about mental health in French with the care the subject deserves: person-first phrasing, useful nuance, and the words that open a conversation rather than close it.

blocks.heading: Person first: the phrasing that respects people
blocks.body: French, like English, has moved towards person-first language. You say "une personne qui vit avec un trouble anxieux", not a label that reduces someone to a diagnosis. Older nouns used as identities are best avoided entirely; "une personne concernée" or "une personne suivie pour…" are the neutral, current forms. The same care applies to verbs: "elle est suivie par un psychologue" is factual and respectful, where colloquial expressions about being "crazy" are not — and are not taught here.

examples.french: C'est une personne qui vit avec un trouble anxieux.
examples.english: This is a person living with an anxiety disorder.

examples.french: Il est suivi par une psychologue depuis six mois.
examples.english: He has been seeing a psychologist for six months.
examples.note: "être suivi par" — the standard, neutral phrase

examples.french: Elle traverse une période difficile.
examples.english: She is going through a difficult period.

examples.french: On parle de personnes concernées, pas de cas.
examples.english: We talk about people affected, not about cases.

examples.french: Le vocabulaire employé peut soigner ou blesser.
examples.english: The vocabulary used can heal or hurt.

blocks.tip: If a French phrase would make you wince in English, it will land the same way in French. When unsure, describe the situation, not the person.

blocks.heading: Naming what is going on, precisely
blocks.body: Precision is part of respect. Le stress is a reaction to a demand; l'anxiété lasts beyond it. Le surmenage is overwork; l'épuisement professionnel — the official French for burnout — is what overwork can lead to. La charge mentale describes the invisible planning load carried at home or at work. Distinguishing these lets you describe an experience accurately instead of reaching for a single dramatic word.

examples.french: Le stress ponctuel n'est pas de l'anxiété chronique.
examples.english: Occasional stress is not chronic anxiety.

examples.french: L'épuisement professionnel se reconnaît à plusieurs signes.
examples.english: Professional burnout can be recognised by several signs.

examples.french: La charge mentale pèse souvent sur les mêmes personnes.
examples.english: The mental load often weighs on the same people.

examples.french: Elle a demandé un aménagement de son poste.
examples.english: She asked for an adjustment to her role.

examples.french: Le sommeil est l'un des premiers indicateurs.
examples.english: Sleep is one of the first indicators.

examples.french: Un mal-être prolongé mérite qu'on en parle à un professionnel.
examples.english: A prolonged sense of unease deserves being discussed with a professional.
examples.note: "le mal-être" is broad and non-clinical — useful in ordinary conversation

blocks.tip: This lesson teaches vocabulary, not diagnosis. Anything that concerns you personally belongs in a conversation with a health professional.

blocks.heading: Opening the conversation, not closing it
blocks.body: The hardest part is often the first sentence. French has a stock of gentle openers that invite without pressing: "comment tu te sens en ce moment ?", "je suis là si tu veux en parler", "tu n'es pas obligé d'en parler maintenant". Notice the pattern — an open question, an offer, and an explicit exit. Avoid the well-meant imperatives ("détends-toi", "pense à autre chose") that shut the subject down. And note the register: this is one of the few areas where even formal French drops into a warmer, simpler tone.

examples.english: Thank you for telling me.

blocks.tip: "Je suis là" — two of the most useful words in the language. Delivered plainly, without advice attached, it is usually enough.

blocks.heading: Softening: the conditional and other cushions
blocks.body: French softens a sensitive question the way English does, but mainly through the conditional. "Tu voudrais en parler ?" is gentler than "tu veux en parler ?", and "il serait peut-être utile de…" suggests without prescribing. Add the standard cushions — peut-être, si tu veux, quand tu te sentiras prêt — and you have a sentence that offers without cornering anyone. The same conditional lets you hedge an observation: "j'ai l'impression que tu es fatigué en ce moment" rather than a flat assertion.

examples.french: Tu voudrais en parler ?
examples.english: Would you like to talk about it?
examples.note: conditional = an offer, not a demand

examples.french: Il serait peut-être utile d'en parler à un professionnel.
examples.english: It might perhaps be useful to talk to a professional about it.

examples.french: J'ai l'impression que tu es fatigué en ce moment.
examples.english: I get the feeling you're tired at the moment.

examples.french: On pourrait en reparler quand tu te sentiras prêt.
examples.english: We could talk about it again when you feel ready.
examples.note: quand + future in French where English uses the present

examples.french: Si tu veux, je t'accompagne au rendez-vous.
examples.english: If you like, I'll come with you to the appointment.

examples.french: Je ne veux surtout pas insister.
examples.english: I really don't want to push.

blocks.tip: The conditional is the politeness engine of French. In this context it does more work than any single vocabulary item.

blocks.heading: Person-first structures: qui, dont, and avoiding labels
blocks.body: Relative clauses are what let you put the person before the condition. "Une personne qui vit avec un trouble anxieux" and "les personnes dont la santé mentale est fragilisée" both keep "personne" as the head noun. Use qui when the person is the subject of the following verb, and dont when the clause would otherwise need de: on parle de sa santé → "une personne dont on parle de la santé" becomes simply "une personne dont la santé…". Note too that the passive être suivi par and the reflexive se sentir describe a situation rather than defining an identity.

examples.french: Une personne qui traverse une période difficile n'est pas définie par elle.
examples.english: A person going through a difficult period is not defined by it.

examples.french: Les personnes dont la santé mentale est fragilisée ont besoin d'écoute.

examples.english: She is a colleague I feel close to.

examples.french: Elle est suivie par une psychologue.
examples.english: She sees a psychologist.
examples.note: être suivi par — factual, neutral, current

examples.french: Je me sens mieux qu'il y a six mois.
examples.english: I feel better than I did six months ago.

examples.french: Ce sont des personnes concernées, pas des étiquettes.
examples.english: They are people affected, not labels.

blocks.tip: Test any sentence by removing the diagnosis: if what remains still describes a whole person, the phrasing is right.

passages.title: La conversation du mardi
passages.french:
Depuis quelques semaines, Malik arrivait au bureau plus tôt et repartait plus tard, sans que son travail avance davantage.
Sa collègue Inès l'avait remarqué, sans savoir quoi en faire : elle ne voulait ni l'ignorer, ni jouer les experts.
Le mardi, en salle de pause, elle a simplement dit : « J'ai l'impression que tu es fatigué en ce moment. »
Malik a haussé les épaules. « Ça va. C'est la période, c'est tout. »
Elle n'a pas insisté. Elle a ajouté une phrase, puis elle s'est tue : « Je suis là si tu veux en parler, et sinon c'est très bien aussi. »
Trois jours plus tard, il est revenu vers elle de lui-même, avec une tasse de café dans chaque main.
Il a parlé du sommeil qui se dérobait, de la charge mentale qui ne s'arrêtait plus le soir, de l'impression de courir sans avancer.
Inès n'a proposé aucune solution. Elle a posé des questions ouvertes et elle a écouté jusqu'au bout.
À un moment, elle a dit : « Tu sais, en parler à un professionnel n'a rien d'un aveu de faiblesse. »
Malik a souri : « C'est étrange, je conseillerais exactement ça à quelqu'un d'autre. »
Il a fini par prendre rendez-vous, non pas à cause de cette conversation, mais peut-être un peu grâce à elle.
Six mois plus tard, il en parle sans détour, avec le recul de quelqu'un qui va mieux et qui le sait.
Ce qui l'a aidé, dit-il, ce n'est pas un conseil brillant, c'est une collègue qui a laissé une porte entrouverte.
Et une phrase, très banale, qu'il n'avait pas entendue depuis longtemps : « Merci de m'en avoir parlé. »
passages.english:
For a few weeks, Malik had been arriving at the office earlier and leaving later, without his work moving on any faster.
His colleague Inès had noticed, without knowing what to do about it: she wanted neither to ignore it nor to play the expert.
On the Tuesday, in the break room, she simply said: "I get the feeling you're tired at the moment."
Malik shrugged. "I'm fine. It's just this time of year, that's all."
She didn't push. She added one sentence, then stopped talking: "I'm here if you want to talk about it, and if not, that's absolutely fine too."
Three days later, he came back to her of his own accord, with a cup of coffee in each hand.
He talked about the sleep that kept slipping away, the mental load that no longer stopped in the evening, the feeling of running without moving forward.
Inès offered no solutions. She asked open questions and listened right to the end.
At one point she said: "You know, talking to a professional is in no way an admission of weakness."
Malik smiled: "It's strange — that's exactly what I'd advise someone else to do."
He eventually made an appointment, not because of that conversation, but perhaps a little thanks to it.
Six months later, he talks about it straightforwardly, with the perspective of someone who is doing better and knows it.
What helped him, he says, was not a brilliant piece of advice; it was a colleague who left a door slightly open.
And one very ordinary sentence he hadn't heard in a long time: "Thank you for telling me."
